name: Aaron Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government, and this conversation is confidential. What does an ordinary day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Aaron Tanaka, 58. I finished a vocational certificate and became a junior lineworker after years in a warehouse. We build and repair power lines for the electricity company; I lay out barriers, test gear with the lead worker, then climb when assigned. I like the careful rhythm of a crew doing a repair right. I am still learning and the height can wear me out by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is waiting at home after a long shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jo works part time at a library, and our two children are grown and out of the house. We have a few months of expenses saved, but I cannot call it a retirement fund. Our union steward, Dev, helped me understand the safety rules when I started. I keep a pocket notebook for fittings and do not use AI tools; I would rather check the manual or ask a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the repair truck still goes out whether software improves or not. If the office saves an hour filing reports, I hope the crew gets that hour back for proper checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still worry about being the slow junior worker at 58. The money we saved covers a few months, but Jo’s library hours change and my knees are not getting younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking my climbing kit against the paper list and take the line shifts on my roster. Starting now I would ask Dev, the union steward, to explain our sick-pay rules; in 2029 I would keep that routine and leave the savings untouched unless we actually lose income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m mostly settled in this picture, with a little worry about my knees. AI hype fading would not make age or variable hours vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the cushion cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months of bills would be comfortable, but we are nearer three at the moment. We will not spend the cushion on a holiday just because the cards look mild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the job must stay careful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trust my lead worker to stop a job when the meter reading is wrong. A tidy report from the office does not replace looking at the wire ourselves.

say: I’d say **repair crews** still need enough time for proper electrical checks.
I’d welcome **shorter reports** if the saved time comes back to the line crew.
think: I’m still a **slow junior** at 58 and worry about my knees.
Our roughly **three-month cushion** could disappear if my shifts or Jo’s library hours fall.
do: Check the **climbing kit** against my paper list and take rostered shifts.
Ask union steward Dev about **sick pay** before an injury happens.
feel: I feel **mostly settled**, with a lingering worry about age and hours.
S0.quote: AI hype fading would not make age or variable hours vanish.
fieldNote: Aaron takes comfort in **paper checks** and a lead worker who can stop unsafe electrical work.
His three months of savings ease the immediate pressure, while **age and variable hours** remain live concerns.

steps.text: Take rostered line shifts and check climbing gear against the paper list
Ask union steward Dev to explain sick-pay rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the office may use AI to schedule jobs, but nobody should cut our safety time to match a screen. I would ask our union to see the new targets before anyone signs off on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer dispatch clerks could mean rougher schedules for us, and Jo’s library may also lose hours if its desk work changes. I can handle a new route sheet, but I dislike a machine deciding how long a live line takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would bring our actual repair times to Dev for the next union meeting. During 2029 I would keep taking line shifts, and if the dispatch tablet became required I would ask the lead worker to walk me through it in paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cross when I imagine a spreadsheet squeezing the work. I am also uneasy because both pay packets could get smaller even while the poles still need repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair would a target get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a broken connector took an extra hour because the fitting was corroded. A route sheet that calls it a twenty-minute job would push a younger worker to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the union to bargain for paid instruction and real repair-time records. I am not volunteering for a night course on a screen the company owns.

say: I’d tell the crew **AI schedules** must not shorten electrical safety checks.
I’d ask our **union** to see new productivity targets before acceptance.
think: I fear **dispatch changes** could push crews to rush and reduce clerk jobs.
Jo’s **library hours** could also shrink, putting both household incomes under pressure.
do: Bring **actual repair times** to Dev for the union meeting.
Ask for **paid tablet instruction** if dispatch screens become required.
Keep taking **line shifts** while the work remains available.
feel: I feel **cross about targets** and uneasy about two uncertain pay packets.
S1.quote: I dislike a machine deciding how long a live line takes.
fieldNote: Aaron moves quickly to a **union meeting** when he imagines unrealistic repair times.
His fear extends beyond his own crew to Jo’s **library desk work**, making the household risk larger.

steps.text: Bring repair-time records to Dev for the next union meeting
Request paid instruction on any required dispatch tablet
Take assigned line shifts through the first year of change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI in 2028 might empty offices, but our line crew still has hands-on repairs until robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the union and company together for a written account of which jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 at the first date and 63 at the robot date. Three months of savings would not carry Jo and me to retirement if my crew went. The library job might already be thinner after thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I would take my payslips and pension paperwork to the union advice session, because I do not know what I am owed. In 2029 I would keep working line shifts, cut the weekend train trips, and apply for the meter-reader vacancy across town if our crew hours fell; before 2031 I would press the union for placement rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel the clock racing in this one. I know I would turn up for work, but my stomach would be tight each time the roster came out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I take a train to see our grown daughter once a month; we would switch to calls if the fare had to go. I would not ask the children to cover our bills unless we had exhausted wages and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a meter-reading role last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The meter-reader vacancy is a possibility, not a guarantee. If robots can do rounds too, I would still need another plan, and I want the company to say so plainly.

say: I’d ask for a **written job plan** from company and union before robots arrive around 2031.
I’d explain **thinking AI** threatens office work in 2028, before line robots reach repairs.
think: Our **three-month savings** cannot bridge the years to retirement if my crew closes.
Jo’s **library income** could shrink even before physical linework changes.
do: Take **payslips and pension papers** to a union advice session this winter.
Keep paid **line shifts** in 2029 while applying for a meter-reader vacancy if hours fall.
Cut **weekend train trips** and press for placement rules before 2031.
feel: I feel **alarmed by the roster** and by the short time to respond.
S2.quote: Three months of savings would not carry Jo and me to retirement if my crew went.
fieldNote: Aaron identifies two dates: **2028 office work** and around 2031 physical line repair by robots.
His fallback meter-reading application is explicitly uncertain, and he seeks **pension facts** before assuming retirement income.

steps.text: Take pension papers to the union session and press for placement rules
Keep taking paid line shifts through 2029
Stop weekend train trips to protect household bills
Apply for the cross-town meter-reader vacancy if crew hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to bargain over changes before the company can simply point at a finished machine. Thinking AI by 2031 will alter the office first; capable line robots around 2034 are the harder question for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I might still have my hands-on job, and at 66 I may still need it. I do not trust a retirement date scribbled on the kitchen calendar without checking our pension and Jo’s hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Dev to put a five-year staffing and paid-training agreement on the union agenda now. I would keep my line certificate current, and in 2032 I would apply for a paid inspection post if people still fill it; before 2034 I would review the pension statement with Jo and decide whether we need another job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary rather than stunned. Years of warning let us act together, but they do not promise that inspection remains human work when robots can climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can keep up with safety refresher training because I have done those classes before. A new inspection role would need paid instruction and a real vacancy, not a motivational poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Jo loses library hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Jo’s library hours dropped, we would stop replacing household things that still work. We would keep the savings for rent and medicine, then revisit the numbers every three months.

say: I’d ask the union to bargain over a **five-year staffing plan** before AGI reaches office work.
I’d explain **robot linework** around 2034 could reach crews still employed after 2031.
think: I may need wages at **66**, and I do not know our pension entitlement yet.
A paid **inspection post** might buy time but could also be automated.
do: Put **staffing and paid training** on the union agenda now.
Apply for **paid inspection work** in 2032 if a human post remains.
Review the **pension statement** with Jo before the robot date.
feel: I feel **wary**, but able to use the warning years with coworkers.
S3.quote: Years of warning let us act together, but they do not promise that inspection remains human work when robots can climb.
fieldNote: Aaron’s longer runway leads first to **collective bargaining**, consistent with his trust in the union.
He does not assume inspection is safe after robots; he wants a **real vacancy** and paid instruction if offered.

steps.text: Ask Dev to put staffing and paid training on the union agenda
Keep the line certificate current through safety refreshers
Apply for a paid human inspection post in 2032 if available
Review the pension statement with Jo before setting a retirement date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade is enough time to demand a decent path out of climbing work. Thinking AI in 2036 could run records, but robots doing repairs around 2039 is when the line crew truly changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking work changes and 71 when robots reach the line. I want retirement before then, but our savings of a few months do not tell me whether that is possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would request my pension estimate in writing and take the ordinary union safety courses while I can still climb. In 2037 I would stay on paid line work if my health allowed, and Jo and I would compare our real income with rent and bills before setting a retirement date; if the numbers fail, I would apply for a less physical depot post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious hope, because ten years might let us step down with some choice. The worry is that my body or the company’s roster gives out before the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a lighter job possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for clearer access to lighter jobs as older workers leave poles. I cannot claim I deserve a depot desk just because I am older; I would need a vacancy and training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move in with the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I have not decided whether to leave this flat after retirement. Our grown children have their own lives, and I would not plan to live with them without asking first.

say: I’d ask for a **path off climbing** during the decade before robots reach line repairs.
I’d distinguish **2036 records** from hands-on robots around 2039.
think: I hope to retire before **71**, but current savings cannot prove we can.
My **health and roster** may change before the technology does.
do: Request a **written pension estimate** and keep taking union safety courses.
Continue **paid line work** in 2037 if healthy.
Apply for a **depot post** if pension figures cannot cover our bills.
feel: I feel **cautiously hopeful**, with health and income still unsettled.
S4.quote: The worry is that my body or the company’s roster gives out before the robot date.
fieldNote: The ten-year warning lets Aaron consider retirement, but he waits for **written pension figures** rather than assuming coverage.
He sees lighter depot work as conditional on a **vacancy and training**, and does not place a burden on grown children.

steps.text: Request a written pension estimate and compare income with bills
Continue paid line shifts in 2037 if health allows
Ask the union for clearer access to lighter jobs for older lineworkers
Apply for a less physical depot post if pension income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The office could change while I am 60, and line robots could reach my crew when I am 63, well before I know whether I can retire. A written placement agreement, paid training for actual openings and honest notice of crew reductions would help Jo and me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether my years in the warehouse were wasted. They taught me to check every box before a truck leaves, which is useful now. I wish I had started the line certificate sooner, but I am here and I intend to do the work safely.

headlineQuote: I wish I had started the line certificate sooner, but I am here and I intend to do the work safely.
portrait: Aaron is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered the trade after warehouse work and still learns from a lead worker.
He and partner Jo have **roughly three months** of expenses saved, while her part-time library hours vary.
He favours **paper safety checks** and union discussion, and has never used AI tools.
Across the scenarios, he seeks **written agreements**, paid instruction and real vacancies while refusing to assume retirement is funded.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Aaron most because line robots could reach his crew while he still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **written placement agreement**, paid training for real openings and notice of crew reductions would help him plan with Jo.
